I-16.explain: Red urine or a positive dipstick is not haematuria until microscopy shows red cells; then the source decides the work-up.

checks.q: What confirms true haematuria?
checks.why: Microscopy proves red cells; dipsticks also react to haemoglobin and myoglobin.

I-16.explain: Glomerular causes leak cells through damaged filters; non-glomerular bleed from the tract below. UTI is the commonest cause overall.
I-16.hook: Filter vs pipes: IgA, PSGN, HSP, Alport above; UTI, stones, trauma, Wilms below.

checks.q: Which is a glomerular cause of haematuria?
checks.why: Alport is a type IV collagen glomerular disease; stones and sickle bleed below the glomerulus.

checks.q: Commonest cause of haematuria overall in children?
checks.why: UTI is the commonest cause overall; IgA is the commonest glomerulonephritis.

I-16.explain: Casts form in tubules, so red cell casts mean the cells entered at the nephron. Timing after sore throat separates IgA from post-strep GN.

checks.q: Which urine finding proves glomerular haematuria?
checks.why: Casts are moulded in tubules, so red cell casts place the bleed in the nephron.

checks.q: Haematuria 1-2 days after URTI with normal complement suggests?
checks.why: IgA is synpharyngitic with normal C3; post-strep comes 1-3 weeks later with low C3.

I-16.explain: Blood that passes the glomerulus is altered to brown and does not clot. Timing in the stream locates lower-tract bleeding.

checks.q: Colour of glomerular haematuria?
checks.why: Glomerular blood is oxidised to brown and lacks clots; clots point to lower tract.

checks.q: Haematuria only at the start of the stream suggests which origin?
checks.why: Initial = urethral; terminal = bladder neck or prostate.

checks.q: Haematuria plus sensorineural deafness suggests?
checks.why: Alport (collagen IV) affects kidney, cochlea and eye; thin BM disease has no deafness.

I-16.explain: A positive dipstick without red cells means a pigment, not blood. In glomerular disease, complement and renal function stage it.
I-16.hook: Dipstick positive, no cells → think pigment.

checks.q: Dipstick blood positive, no red cells on microscopy suggests?
checks.why: Haem pigments react with the dipstick; beetroot and rifampicin colour urine but are dipstick negative.

checks.q: Key blood test in glomerular haematuria?
checks.why: Low C3 points to post-strep GN, MPGN or lupus; normal C3 to IgA.

I-16.explain: Once casts prove a glomerular source, cystoscopy is pointless. Non-glomerular causes are treated directly.

checks.q: Red cell casts found: next direction of work-up?
checks.why: Casts localise to the glomerulus, so stop investigating the bladder.

checks.q: Wilms tumour typically spreads to which organ?
checks.why: Wilms metastasises mostly to the lungs; neuroblastoma favours bone and marrow.

I-17.explain: Bladder control is expected by 5, so wetting is only labelled enuresis after that age and when frequent and persistent.

checks.q: Minimum age to diagnose enuresis?
checks.why: Enuresis needs age ≥ 5 with wetting ≥ 2 times/week for ≥ 3 months.

I-17.explain: Nocturnal enuresis is strongly inherited. Secondary enuresis (after 6 dry months) needs a cause such as UTI or diabetes.
I-17.hook: Both parents wet → 7 in 10 kids wet.

checks.q: Greatest risk factor for primary enuresis?
checks.why: Genetics dominates: both parents affected gives ~70% risk.

checks.q: Which is a cause of secondary enuresis?
checks.why: New wetting after being dry suggests UTI, DM, DI, constipation or stress.

I-17.explain: Three mechanisms: the child does not wake, makes too much night urine (low ADH), or has a small bladder. A full rectum irritates the bladder.

checks.q: Nocturnal polyuria in enuresis reflects low levels of?
checks.why: Inadequate nocturnal ADH rise causes high night urine volume, the basis for desmopressin.

checks.q: How does constipation cause wetting?
checks.why: A loaded rectum compresses the bladder, triggering overactive detrusor contractions.

I-17.explain: Constant dribbling despite normal voiding means urine bypasses the sphincter, classically an ectopic ureter in girls.
I-17.hook: Always damp girl = ureter in the wrong place.

checks.q: Continuous dampness in a toilet-trained girl suggests?
checks.why: An ectopic ureter entering below the sphincter drips constantly; valves occur in boys.

checks.q: Sacral dimple with hairy patch in an enuretic child suggests?
checks.why: Cutaneous lumbosacral markers signal occult spinal dysraphism (tethered cord).

I-17.explain: Rule out organic causes cheaply: dipstick and a focused neuro exam catch most.

checks.q: First investigation for every enuretic child?
checks.why: Dipstick screens for infection, glucose and concentrating ability (specific gravity).

checks.q: Which examination is key in enuresis?
checks.why: Spine, gait and lower-limb reflexes screen for neurogenic bladder.

I-17.explain: Start with behavioural measures; add alarm (conditioning, lasting cure) or desmopressin (fast, but relapse). Desmopressin + fluids risks hyponatraemia.

checks.q: First-line treatment of enuresis?
checks.why: Behavioural measures first: evening fluid restriction and timed voiding.

checks.q: Which drug is now rarely used for enuresis?
checks.why: Imipramine is rarely used because of cardiotoxicity in overdose.

checks.q: Main risk if fluids aren't restricted on desmopressin?
checks.why: Desmopressin retains free water; evening drinking causes dilutional hyponatraemia.

I-18.explain: Polyuria is defined by body surface area so it scales across ages.
I-18.hook: Over 2 litres per m² per day.

checks.q: Threshold for true polyuria in children?
checks.why: Polyuria is >2 l/m²/day.

I-18.explain: Too much solute (glucose), no ADH effect (DI), or too much drinking. Central DI lesions sit in the hypothalamus/pituitary.

checks.q: Commonest osmotic cause of polyuria?
checks.why: Glycosuria drives osmotic diuresis; DM is the classic cause.

checks.q: Which tumour classically causes central DI in children?
checks.why: Craniopharyngioma and germinoma involve the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.

checks.q: Which electrolyte abnormality causes nephrogenic DI?
checks.why: High Ca and low K impair renal concentrating ability.

I-18.explain: Central DI lacks ADH; nephrogenic has ADH but the kidney cannot respond. Compulsive drinkers dilute their plasma.
I-18.hook: Central = no signal; nephrogenic = deaf receiver.

checks.q: In nephrogenic DI, ADH levels are typically?
checks.why: The kidney ignores ADH, so ADH is normal or raised.

checks.q: Serum osmolality in primary polydipsia?
checks.why: Excess water intake dilutes plasma; DI raises serum osmolality.

I-18.explain: Glucose in urine plus weight loss despite eating means insulin lack. DI loses free water so plasma concentrates while urine stays dilute.

checks.q: Weight loss despite good appetite, glycosuria and ketones suggest?
checks.why: Insulin deficiency causes catabolism, glycosuria and ketosis.

checks.q: Typical DI laboratory pattern?
checks.why: Free water loss concentrates plasma while urine cannot concentrate.

I-18.explain: Dipstick excludes DM in seconds. The water deprivation test is stopped early to avoid dangerous dehydration; desmopressin response separates central from nephrogenic.
I-18.hook: Responds to DDAVP → brain is the problem → MRI.

checks.q: First bedside test in polyuria?
checks.why: Dipstick for glucose first; then paired serum and urine osmolality.

checks.q: When is the water deprivation test stopped?
checks.why: Stop at 3-5% weight loss to prevent severe dehydration.

checks.q: Urine concentrates after desmopressin: next step?
checks.why: Response means central DI, so image the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.

I-18.explain: Central DI replaces the missing hormone, and other pituitary hormones may also be lost. Nephrogenic DI cannot use ADH, so reduce solute load and use thiazides.
I-18.hook: Paradox: a diuretic (thiazide) reduces urine in nephrogenic DI.

checks.q: Treatment of central DI?
checks.why: Replace ADH with desmopressin; also check cortisol and other pituitary axes.

checks.q: Which drug class paradoxically helps nephrogenic DI?
checks.why: Thiazides cause mild volume depletion, increasing proximal reabsorption.

I-19.explain: Childhood BP norms vary with age, sex and height, so centiles are used and repeated readings avoid white-coat errors. Phaeo follows the rule of 10s.

checks.q: Hypertension threshold in children?
checks.why: BP ≥ 95th centile for age, sex and height on 3 occasions.

checks.q: Phaeochromocytoma arises from which cells?
checks.why: Phaeo is a catecholamine-secreting chromaffin cell tumour (rule of 10s).

I-19.explain: Unlike adults, most childhood hypertension is secondary, mainly renal. Phaeo associates with inherited tumour syndromes.
I-19.hook: Child BP high? Look at the kidney.

checks.q: Most frequent cause of hypertension before adolescence?
checks.why: Renal parenchymal disease causes ~70-80% (matches university key).

checks.q: Which polycystic kidney disease presents in infancy?
checks.why: ARPKD (PKHD1) presents in infants; ADPKD in young adults.

checks.q: Which syndrome is linked to phaeochromocytoma?
checks.why: MEN 2A/2B, VHL, NF1 and SDH mutations; MEN 1 gives parathyroid, pancreas, pituitary.

I-19.explain: Catecholamine bursts cause paroxysms. Blocking beta first leaves alpha vasoconstriction unopposed. Neuroblastoma is the childhood adrenal medulla tumour.
I-19.hook: Alpha before beta, like the alphabet.

checks.q: Phaeochromocytoma symptoms are typically?
checks.why: Catecholamine surges produce paroxysmal attacks.

checks.q: Giving a beta-blocker first in phaeo risks?
checks.why: Unopposed alpha vasoconstriction triggers a hypertensive crisis.

checks.q: Which oncogene is linked to neuroblastoma?
checks.why: N-myc amplification marks poor prognosis; WT1 is Wilms.

I-19.explain: Catecholamines cause headache, sweating, palpitations and hyperglycaemia. Pulse and phenotype clues point to other causes.

checks.q: Classic phaeo triad includes headache, palpitations and?
checks.why: Episodic headache, sweating and palpitations; flushing suggests carcinoid.

checks.q: Hypertension with weak femoral pulses suggests?
checks.why: Coarctation reduces lower-limb perfusion: weak, delayed femorals.

checks.q: Which feature suggests MEN 2B?
checks.why: MEN 2B: marfanoid habitus, kyphoscoliosis, mucosal neuromas.

I-19.explain: A small cuff overestimates BP. Phaeo is confirmed biochemically before imaging. Renal imaging finds PKD and FMD.

checks.q: Correct BP cuff bladder covers what share of arm circumference?
checks.why: Bladder should cover 80% of arm; too small falsely raises BP.

checks.q: First test for suspected phaeochromocytoma?
checks.why: Confirm with metanephrines, then CT/MRI, then I-123 MIBG.

checks.q: 'String of beads' on angiography indicates?
checks.why: FMD gives alternating stenoses and dilatations.

I-19.explain: Block alpha first, then beta, then operate. Hyperkinetic (high output) hypertension responds to beta-blockers; Cushing triad BP maintains brain perfusion.
I-19.hook: Cushing triad: don't drop the BP, drop the ICP.

checks.q: First drug in preoperative phaeochromocytoma management?
checks.why: Alpha-blockade with phenoxybenzamine first, then beta-blockade, then surgery.

checks.q: Drug of choice for hyperkinetic hypertension?
checks.why: Beta-blockers reduce high cardiac output (university key).

I-20.explain: Duration separates self-limiting infection from persistent disease; the 3-4 week gap is the subacute zone.

checks.q: Chronic cough in children lasts more than?
checks.why: Chronic cough lasts >4 weeks; acute <3 weeks (adults use 8 weeks).

I-20.explain: Acute cough is usually viral. Chronic cough needs a specific diagnosis; asthma is common but not the only cause.

checks.q: Most common cause of acute cough?
checks.why: Viral URTI is commonest (university key).

checks.q: Which is a cause of chronic cough?
checks.why: PBB is chronic wet cough; croup and bronchiolitis are acute.

I-20.explain: Bronchiolitis inflames small airways. Pertussis runs in three phases. Wet cough plus clubbing means suppuration (CF, bronchiectasis).

checks.q: Usual cause of bronchiolitis?
checks.why: RSV causes most bronchiolitis; parainfluenza causes croup.

checks.q: First phase of pertussis?
checks.why: Catarrhal (1-2 weeks) → paroxysmal → convalescent.

checks.q: Chronic wet cough with clubbing suggests?
checks.why: Clubbing points to CF or bronchiectasis, never asthma.

I-20.explain: The sound of the cough and the context point to the diagnosis. Infants with pertussis may only have apnoea.
I-20.hook: Bark = croup; whoop = pertussis; sudden = foreign body.

checks.q: Young infants with pertussis may present with?
checks.why: Infants often lack the whoop and present with apnoea or cyanosis.

checks.q: Barking cough suggests?
checks.why: Barking seal-like cough = croup (laryngotracheitis).

checks.q: Sudden cough in a previously well toddler suggests?
checks.why: Abrupt onset in a well toddler = foreign body until proven otherwise.

I-20.explain: Growth, clubbing and history identify serious chronic disease. Radiolucent foreign bodies don't show on X-ray.
I-20.hook: Normal CXR doesn't clear a foreign body.

checks.q: Which history item is key in chronic cough?
checks.why: A choking history suggests foreign body; also check growth, clubbing, TB contacts.

checks.q: Suspected foreign body with normal CXR: next step?
checks.why: Most foreign bodies are radiolucent; rigid bronchoscopy diagnoses and removes.

I-20.explain: Viral cough resolves alone; OTC cough medicines are ineffective and risky. Pertussis antibiotics mainly cut spread.
I-20.hook: Pertussis: macrolide for patient and contacts.

checks.q: Management of viral cough in children?
checks.why: OTC cough medicines are not recommended in children.

checks.q: RSV prevention in infants uses?
checks.why: Monoclonal antibodies nirsevimab or palivizumab prevent RSV.

checks.q: Treatment of pertussis?
checks.why: Macrolides (azithromycin) for case and close contacts.

I-21.explain: Most sore throats are viral; the clinical job is to find group A strep because it causes rheumatic fever.
I-21.hook: Hunt the strep among the viruses.

checks.q: Proportion of childhood sore throats that are viral?
checks.why: 70-80% are viral; the aim is finding group A strep.

I-21.explain: Strep peaks in school age; EBV in teens. Some throats are airway emergencies.

checks.q: Peak age range for streptococcal pharyngitis?
checks.why: Group A strep is commonest age 3-14; rare under 3.

checks.q: Which sore-throat cause is an emergency?
checks.why: Epiglottitis, quinsy, retropharyngeal abscess, diphtheria and Lemierre are emergencies.

I-21.explain: Antibiotics prevent rheumatic fever (cross-reactive antibodies) but not PSGN (immune complexes). Catarrhal symptoms imply a virus.
I-21.hook: Antibiotics stop the heart damage, not the kidney damage.

checks.q: Antibiotics for strep throat prevent which complication?
checks.why: Treatment prevents rheumatic fever; PSGN is not prevented.

checks.q: Sore throat with cough and coryza suggests?
checks.why: Cough, coryza and hoarseness point to a virus.

I-21.explain: Strep: fever, exudate, tender anterior nodes, no cough. Deep neck infections show trismus or airway signs.

checks.q: Which feature favours EBV over strep?
checks.why: EBV: posterior cervical nodes and splenomegaly.

checks.q: In quinsy, the uvula deviates?
checks.why: Peritonsillar abscess pushes the uvula to the opposite side, with trismus.

I-21.explain: A negative rapid test can miss strep, so culture follows. EBV and diphtheria have tell-tale lab or exam signs.

checks.q: Rapid strep test negative: next step?
checks.why: Rapid antigen tests have low sensitivity; confirm negatives with culture.

checks.q: Grey-white adherent pseudomembrane suggests?
checks.why: Diphtheria forms a grey pseudomembrane that bleeds on removal.

I-21.explain: Ten days of penicillin eradicates strep to prevent rheumatic fever. Amoxicillin in EBV causes a rash; the spleen can rupture.
I-21.hook: EBV + amoxicillin = rash; spleen = no rugby.

checks.q: Treatment for streptococcal pharyngitis?
checks.why: Penicillin V for 10 days to prevent rheumatic fever.

checks.q: EBV: how long to avoid contact sports?
checks.why: Avoid contact sport 4-6 weeks due to splenic rupture risk.

I-22.explain: Stridor in inspiration means the narrowing is above the thoracic inlet, where negative pressure collapses the airway.

checks.q: Inspiratory stridor localises obstruction to?
checks.why: Inspiratory stridor = extrathoracic obstruction; acute cause usually croup.

I-22.explain: Croup is a viral laryngotracheitis of young children. Mimics include bacterial and structural causes.

checks.q: Commonest cause of croup?
checks.why: Parainfluenza; typical age 6 months to 6 years.

checks.q: Bacterial tracheitis is usually caused by?
checks.why: Staph aureus is the classic cause of bacterial tracheitis.

I-22.explain: The cricoid is a complete ring, so swelling can only go inward, narrowing the subglottis.

checks.q: Why does subglottic swelling narrow the airway so much?
checks.why: The cricoid is the only complete cartilage ring, so oedema can only narrow the lumen.

I-22.explain: Croup: bark, stridor, not toxic. Toxic children with drooling or no response to adrenaline have a bacterial cause.

checks.q: Stridor that improves lying prone suggests?
checks.why: Laryngomalacia improves prone and worsens supine or with crying.

checks.q: Toxic child with stridor not responding to adrenaline suggests?
checks.why: Bacterial tracheitis: toxic and unresponsive to nebulised adrenaline.

I-22.explain: Severity is clinical; saturation drops late. In epiglottitis throat examination can trigger complete obstruction.

checks.q: Which is NOT used to grade croup severity?
checks.why: Severity uses stridor at rest, recession and conscious level; hypoxia is late.

checks.q: Suspected epiglottitis: what must you avoid?
checks.why: Throat examination can precipitate complete airway obstruction.

I-22.explain: Steroids reduce oedema for every croup; adrenaline gives fast but short relief, so observe afterwards. Epiglottitis needs a secured airway.
I-22.hook: Adrenaline lasts ~2 hours: watch for rebound.

checks.q: Nebulised adrenaline effect in croup wears off after about?
checks.why: Effect lasts about 2 hours, so observe for rebound. (Steroid route: university key accepts rectal steroid.)

checks.q: First priority in epiglottitis?
checks.why: Secure the airway first, in theatre with anaesthetics and ENT.

I-23.explain: Red cell destruction triggers marrow response (reticulocytes) and releases haem (bilirubin, LDH) while haptoglobin is consumed.

checks.q: Which marker is low in haemolysis?
checks.why: Haptoglobin binds free Hb and is consumed; retics, bilirubin, LDH rise.

I-23.explain: The Coombs test splits immune from non-immune haemolysis.
I-23.hook: Warm = IgG; cold = IgM (M for 'chilly Mountain').

checks.q: Antibody class in warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia?
checks.why: Warm AIHA is IgG; cold AIHA is IgM.

checks.q: Which haemolytic anaemia is Coombs negative?
checks.why: HS is a membrane defect, not immune, so DAT is negative.

I-23.explain: Spherocytosis: weak membrane tethering makes rigid spheres trapped in the spleen. G6PD cells can't resist oxidant stress.

checks.q: Inheritance of hereditary spherocytosis?
checks.why: HS is mostly autosomal dominant; G6PD is X-linked.

checks.q: Bite cells and Heinz bodies after fava beans suggest?
checks.why: Oxidant stress denatures Hb (Heinz bodies) that the spleen bites out.

I-23.explain: Haemolysis causes jaundice and splenomegaly. Parvovirus halts erythropoiesis, which haemolytic patients can't tolerate.
I-23.hook: Low retics in a haemolyser = parvovirus.

checks.q: Painful swollen hands in a sickle cell infant?
checks.why: Dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome) is often the first sickle crisis.

checks.q: Sudden low reticulocytes in chronic haemolysis suggest?
checks.why: Parvovirus B19 infects erythroid precursors, causing aplastic crisis.

I-23.explain: HS shows spherocytes, raised MCHC and positive EMA binding. Fragmented cells mean mechanical destruction.

checks.q: Confirmatory test for hereditary spherocytosis?
checks.why: EMA binding (flow cytometry) is positive; DAT is negative.

checks.q: Schistocytes on film indicate?
checks.why: Fragmented cells = MAHA (HUS, TTP, DIC).

I-23.explain: Warm AIHA responds to steroids. Asplenic sickle children need penicillin and urgent antibiotics for fever.

checks.q: First-line drug treatment for warm AIHA?
checks.why: Stop offending drugs, give steroids; splenectomy last resort.

checks.q: Sickle cell: daily penicillin until what age?
checks.why: Prophylactic penicillin to 5 years for functional asplenia.

I-24.explain: MCV sorts anaemias into micro-, normo- and macrocytic. Iron deficiency is commonest.

checks.q: First branch point in classifying anaemia?
checks.why: MCV first; iron deficiency is the commonest childhood anaemia.

I-24.explain: Small cells: iron, thalassaemia, lead. Large cells: B12/folate, Diamond-Blackfan. All lines low: Fanconi, aplastic.

checks.q: Which causes microcytic anaemia?
checks.why: Lead, iron deficiency and thal trait are microcytic.

checks.q: Which causes inherited pancytopenia?
checks.why: Fanconi is inherited marrow failure; DBA affects red cells only.

I-24.explain: Cow's milk is iron-poor, blocks iron absorption and causes occult GI blood loss. Without B12/folate, DNA lags and cells grow large.
I-24.hook: Too much milk, too little iron.

checks.q: Classic dietary cause of iron deficiency in toddlers?
checks.why: Cow's milk is iron-poor, inhibits absorption and causes occult blood loss.

checks.q: Why are cells large in B12 deficiency?
checks.why: Nuclear maturation lags behind cytoplasm, giving megaloblasts.

I-24.explain: Lead leaves a gum line and neuro signs; B12 causes neuropathy. Fanconi carries skeletal and skin anomalies.

checks.q: Bluish gum-tooth line suggests?
checks.why: Lead lines (Burton line) on the gums.

checks.q: Malformed thumbs and short stature with anaemia suggest?
checks.why: Fanconi: thumb/radial anomalies, short stature, café-au-lait spots.

I-24.explain: Iron deficiency makes cells of varying size (high RDW); thal trait makes many uniform small cells. Ferritin rises in inflammation.
I-24.hook: Thal trait: many small even cells.

checks.q: RDW in thalassaemia trait is typically?
checks.why: Normal RDW with normal/high RBC count; high RDW suggests iron deficiency.

checks.q: Why can ferritin be normal despite iron deficiency?
checks.why: Inflammation raises ferritin, masking deficiency.

I-24.explain: Continue iron after Hb normalises to refill stores. Chelation intensity scales with blood lead.
I-24.hook: Iron: 3 more months to fill the tank.

checks.q: Continue oral iron how long after Hb normalises?
checks.why: Continue 3 months to replenish iron stores.

checks.q: Blood lead 45-69 mcg/dL is treated with?
checks.why: DMSA for 45-69; ≥ 70 needs dimercaprol + EDTA.

I-25.explain: Downward crossing of centiles shows growth falling below the child's own trajectory.

checks.q: FTT classically means crossing how many weight centiles downward?
checks.why: Crossing ≥ 2 major weight centile lines downward.

I-25.explain: Most FTT is not enough food in. Organic causes include malabsorption, metabolic and cardiac disease.
I-25.hook: Not enough in, before rare diseases.

checks.q: Commonest cause of failure to thrive?
checks.why: Non-organic inadequate intake; neglect is the commonest maltreatment.

checks.q: Which is an organic cause of FTT?
checks.why: Galactosaemia, CF and congenital heart disease cause organic FTT.

I-25.explain: Undernutrition hits weight first, then height, sparing the head longest. Heart disease raises needs and reduces feeding.

checks.q: Which is lost last in undernutrition?
checks.why: Weight → height → head circumference.

checks.q: Why do infants with congenital heart disease fail to thrive?
checks.why: Increased work of breathing and tachycardia raise expenditure while feeding tires them.

I-25.explain: Short but plump points to hormone problems, not starvation. Early small head points to prenatal causes. Kwashiorkor = protein lack with oedema.

checks.q: Short, plump child with delayed bone age suggests?
checks.why: Hypothyroidism, GH deficiency or Cushing keep weight but stunt height.

checks.q: Small head from early infancy suggests?
checks.why: Early microcephaly reflects prenatal insults or genetic causes.

checks.q: Oedema with swollen abdomen in malnutrition indicates?
checks.why: Kwashiorkor: protein deficiency with oedema; marasmus is wasting.

I-25.explain: Watching a feed reveals technique and interaction problems that no test can.

checks.q: Highest-yield 'investigation' in failure to thrive?
checks.why: Observing a feed often reveals the problem.

checks.q: Neonatal jaundice with E. coli sepsis suggests?
checks.why: Galactosaemia predisposes to E. coli sepsis; meconium ileus → CF.

I-25.explain: Management targets the cause; feeding advice for intake. Suspected abuse is a safeguarding referral first.

checks.q: First-line management of FTT from poor intake?
checks.why: Treat the cause; feeding advice for intake problems.

checks.q: Suspected abuse in FTT: first contact?
checks.why: Notify child protective services first.

I-26.explain: Infant livers are often palpable below the costal margin, so span, not edge, defines enlargement.

checks.q: How to assess hepatomegaly in infants?
checks.why: A palpable edge is normal in infants; measure the span.

I-26.explain: Infections (EBV, CMV, malaria, leishmaniasis), haemolysis, inflammation and storage disease enlarge liver and spleen.

checks.q: Which infection causes hepatosplenomegaly?
checks.why: Leishmaniasis, malaria, EBV and CMV cause hepatosplenomegaly.

checks.q: Which glycogen storage disease causes hepatomegaly?
checks.why: Type I (von Gierke) causes hepatomegaly and fasting hypoglycaemia.

I-26.explain: The spleen must be substantially enlarged before palpable. Big spleens trap cells, lowering counts.

checks.q: Spleen must enlarge how much before palpable?
checks.why: Roughly 2-3 times normal size before palpable.

checks.q: Hypersplenism typically lowers which count?
checks.why: Sequestration lowers platelets (and other cells).

I-26.explain: Von Gierke cannot release glucose from glycogen. CMV causes extramedullary haematopoiesis (blueberry muffin rash).

checks.q: Infant hepatomegaly with fasting hypoglycaemia suggests?
checks.why: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency traps glycogen in the liver.

checks.q: Spiking fevers with salmon-pink rash suggest?
checks.why: Systemic JIA: quotidian fever with evanescent salmon rash.

I-26.explain: The blood film shows haemolysis, leukaemia or atypical lymphocytes. INR reflects liver synthesis; ALT reflects injury.

checks.q: First test in hepatosplenomegaly?
checks.why: FBC and film first.

checks.q: Best marker of liver synthetic function?
checks.why: PT/INR reflects clotting factor synthesis; ALT reflects injury.

I-26.explain: No organomegaly-specific treatment: manage the cause. EBV spleens are fragile.
I-26.hook: EBV spleen: no contact sport 4-6 weeks.

checks.q: Management principle in hepatosplenomegaly?
checks.why: Treat the underlying cause.

checks.q: EBV splenomegaly: avoid contact sport for?
checks.why: Avoid contact sports 4-6 weeks (splenic rupture).

I-27.explain: Dehydration kills in diarrhoea, so hydration status outranks stool details.
I-27.hook: Look at the child, not the nappy.

checks.q: Priority in acute diarrhoea?
checks.why: Assess hydration first.

I-27.explain: Viruses cause most acute diarrhoea; blood suggests bacteria. In chronic diarrhoea growth separates benign from serious.

checks.q: Commonest causes of acute diarrhoea in children?
checks.why: Mostly viral; bacterial if bloody.

checks.q: Pivotal question in chronic diarrhoea?
checks.why: Growth separates toddler's diarrhoea from coeliac, CF, IBD.

I-27.explain: SGLT1 co-transports sodium with glucose even in infected gut, so ORS works. Antibiotics release Shiga toxin. Osmotic diarrhoea needs intake.

checks.q: Why does ORS work in gastroenteritis?
checks.why: Sodium-glucose cotransport is preserved, pulling water with it.

checks.q: Antibiotics in E. coli O157 raise risk of?
checks.why: Antibiotics increase Shiga toxin release → HUS.

checks.q: Diarrhoea continuing during fasting is?
checks.why: Secretory continues; osmotic stops with fasting.

I-27.explain: Rapid transit in a thriving toddler shows undigested food. Blood and high fever point to invasive bacteria.
I-27.hook: Peas and carrots in the nappy = toddler's.

checks.q: Recognisable food in stools of a thriving 2-year-old?
checks.why: Toddler's diarrhoea: thriving child, undigested food.

checks.q: Which feature suggests bacterial diarrhoea?
checks.why: Blood, high fever and severe pain suggest bacteria.

I-27.explain: Dehydration is graded clinically. Faltering growth needs coeliac, CF and IBD screening; total IgA avoids false-negative tTG.

checks.q: How is dehydration graded?
checks.why: Dehydration is graded clinically.

checks.q: Why measure total IgA with tTG?
checks.why: tTG-IgA is falsely negative in IgA deficiency.

I-27.explain: ORS plus continued feeding is first-line; IV only if ORS fails. Antimotility drugs and routine antibiotics are avoided.
I-27.hook: ORS first, IV if it fails.

checks.q: First-line treatment of dehydrating gastroenteritis?
checks.why: ORS and continue feeding; IV only if ORS fails.

checks.q: Use of loperamide in children with diarrhoea?
checks.why: Loperamide is not used in children; no routine antibiotics.

I-28.explain: Bile enters at the ampulla of Vater, so bilious vomit means the blockage lies beyond it.

checks.q: Bilious vomiting means obstruction distal to?
checks.why: Bile enters at the ampulla, so obstruction is distal to it.

I-28.explain: Age determines the likely cause: congenital obstruction in neonates, pyloric stenosis and intussusception in infants.

checks.q: Which endocrine disorder causes neonatal vomiting?
checks.why: Salt-wasting CAH causes vomiting, shock and electrolyte disturbance.

checks.q: Which causes vomiting in an infant of 2 months?
checks.why: Pyloric stenosis peaks at 2-8 weeks.

I-28.explain: Vomiting gastric acid loses H+ and Cl-. Kidneys save sodium by swapping K+ and H+, so urine is acidic.
I-28.hook: Pyloric: low Cl, low K, alkalosis.

checks.q: Acid-base picture in pyloric stenosis?
checks.why: Loss of HCl gives hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic alkalosis.

checks.q: Urine pH in late pyloric stenosis despite alkalosis?
checks.why: Paradoxical aciduria: kidneys excrete H+ to retain Na+ and K+.

I-28.explain: Hypertrophied pylorus blocks gastric outflow without bile: projectile vomit, hungry after. CAH loses aldosterone: low Na, high K.

checks.q: Typical age of pyloric stenosis?
checks.why: Presents at 2-8 weeks, firstborn boys.

checks.q: Neonate with shock, low sodium, high potassium?
checks.why: Aldosterone deficiency gives hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia.

I-28.explain: Volvulus can necrose the midgut within hours, so bilious vomiting is urgent. Ultrasound shows the thick pylorus.
I-28.hook: Bilious vomit = rule out volvulus now.

checks.q: Bilious vomiting in a neonate: urgent exclusion of?
checks.why: Midgut volvulus must be excluded urgently.

checks.q: Imaging of choice for pyloric stenosis?
checks.why: Ultrasound (university key).

I-28.explain: Pyloric stenosis is not an emergency operation: correct the alkalosis first. Volvulus is.
I-28.hook: Fix the fluids, then the pylorus.

checks.q: Why correct alkalosis before pyloromyotomy?
checks.why: Alkalosis depresses respiratory drive, risking post-op apnoea.

checks.q: Operation for pyloric stenosis?
checks.why: Ramstedt pyloromyotomy; Ladd procedure is for malrotation.

I-29.explain: Appendicitis is the commonest surgical acute abdomen in children.

checks.q: Most common cause of acute abdomen in children?
checks.why: Appendicitis (university key).

I-29.explain: Age narrows the list: NEC/volvulus in neonates, intussusception in toddlers, appendicitis in school age, torsion in adolescents.
I-29.hook: Neonate NEC, toddler telescopes, schoolkid appendix.

checks.q: Typical acute abdomen cause in a toddler?
checks.why: Intussusception peaks in toddlers; NEC in neonates.

checks.q: Which is an acute abdomen cause in adolescents?
checks.why: Adolescents: testicular or ovarian torsion, gynaecological causes.

I-29.explain: Early appendix pain is visceral, referred to the umbilicus via T10. Splenic rupture may be delayed after a subcapsular haematoma.
I-29.hook: Appendix starts at the belly button (T10).

checks.q: Why does appendicitis pain start periumbilically?
checks.why: The appendix is midgut; visceral afferents enter at T10.

checks.q: Second stage of two-stage splenic rupture?
options: Sudden shock hours to days later
checks.why: Subcapsular haematoma ruptures later causing rapid shock (university key).

I-29.explain: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is volvulus until proven otherwise. Appendicitis pain migrates as the parietal peritoneum is irritated.

checks.q: Neonate with bilious vomiting: presume?
checks.why: Malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise.

checks.q: Typical appendicitis fever?
checks.why: Low fever; high fever suggests perforation or other cause.

I-29.explain: Cheap checks catch mimics: pneumonia, UTI, DKA and torsion. Polytrauma gets whole-body CT.

checks.q: Which 'free check' catches DKA in abdominal pain?
checks.why: Glucose detects DKA presenting as abdominal pain.

checks.q: Imaging study for the polytraumatised child?
checks.why: Acute CT (university key); selective CT is now preferred to limit radiation.

I-29.explain: Peritonism needs a surgeon; resuscitate first if unstable. Torsion is time-critical.

checks.q: Child with peritonism: management?
checks.why: Peritonism → surgical referral; resuscitate if unstable.

checks.q: Testicular salvage falls sharply after about?
checks.why: Salvage drops markedly after about 6 hours.

I-30.explain: Rule out benign causes (bladder, faeces, hydronephrosis), then distinguish the two big tumours.

checks.q: Main malignant differential of an abdominal mass in a child?
checks.why: Exclude benign causes, then separate Wilms from neuroblastoma.

I-30.explain: Neonatal masses are mostly renal. Wilms links to WT1 syndromes; neuroblastoma arises from neural crest.
I-30.hook: WAGR: Wilms, Aniridia, GU anomalies, Retardation.

checks.q: Most neonatal abdominal masses arise from?
checks.why: Most neonatal masses are renal: hydronephrosis, MCDK.

checks.q: Aniridia is associated with which tumour?
checks.why: WAGR syndrome includes Wilms and aniridia.

I-30.explain: Wilms arises from persistent metanephric blastema; it spreads to the lungs. Its capsule can rupture with palpation, upstaging it.

checks.q: Wilms tumour arises from?
checks.why: Metanephric blastema; neuroblastoma is neural crest.

checks.q: Why avoid repeated palpation of a renal mass?
checks.why: Rupture spills tumour and upstages Wilms.

I-30.explain: Wilms: older, well, smooth, stays on one side. Neuroblastoma: younger, unwell, crosses midline, paraneoplastic and periorbital signs.

checks.q: Peak age of Wilms tumour?
checks.why: Wilms peaks at 3-4 years; neuroblastoma under 2.

checks.q: Opsoclonus-myoclonus suggests?
checks.why: Paraneoplastic opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia is classic for neuroblastoma.

I-30.explain: Ultrasound is safe and shows organ of origin. Neuroblastoma secretes catecholamine metabolites.

checks.q: First imaging for a palpable abdominal mass?
checks.why: Ultrasound first.

checks.q: Raised urinary VMA and HVA suggest?
checks.why: Catecholamine metabolites are raised in neuroblastoma.

I-30.explain: Avoid palpation. Europe gives chemo first to shrink the tumour; the US operates first for staging.
I-30.hook: SIOP: chemo first; COG: cut first.

checks.q: Suspected Wilms: what must be avoided?
checks.why: Repeated palpation risks rupture.

checks.q: European (SIOP) approach to Wilms tumour?
checks.why: SIOP gives pre-op chemo; COG usually operates first.
